findings.claim: should_encode's `masked_text` branch has zero test coverage, in either plain or Packed form. CHANGES.md claims this is a pure refactor where 'every column kind that used to be picked up by the alias-list call is still picked up here, and nothing else is,' but the fixture table in test_columnstore.py never includes a masked_text column (plain or Packed), so that claim is unverified for one of the three encoded kinds.
findings.source: test_columnstore.py:17-25 (`_table()` fixture: columns are name/text, age/number, grade/choice, packed_name/Packed(text), packed_grade/Packed(choice) -- no masked_text) vs columnstore.py:64 `return kind in {"text", "masked_text", "choice"}`
findings.remedy: Add a masked_text column and a Packed("masked_text") column to _table() and assert both appear in encode_categoricals(), matching the coverage already given to text and choice.

findings.claim: The Packed-unwrapping expression is duplicated verbatim in column_subset and should_encode. The module docstring itself commits these two functions to the same unwrapping behavior ('should_encode unwraps a Packed kind to the primitive it packs the same way column_subset does'), so this is one policy expressed at two sites, not two similar-looking pieces of code that are free to diverge -- exactly the case where consolidating is the fix, per the same-policy rule. If a second wrapper type is ever added, one site can be updated and the other missed, silently breaking the 'same set of columns' invariant CHANGES.md relies on.
findings.source: columnstore.py:53 `alias = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind` (in column_subset) vs columnstore.py:63 `kind = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind` (in should_encode); shared-policy claim at columnstore.py:6-8
findings.remedy: Extract a single helper, e.g. `def _primitive(kind: str | Packed) -> str: return kind.primitive if isinstance(kind, Packed) else kind`, and call it from both column_subset and should_encode.

findings.claim: describe_source checks whether a layer carries a key by truthiness (`env.get(key)`), while effective_value checks by presence (`key in env`). The module's own docstring defines carrying as presence regardless of value: 'A layer "carries" a key when the key is present, whatever the value -- an explicitly empty string is a deliberate override, not an absence.' So for a key explicitly set to "" in a higher-precedence layer, effective_value correctly returns that empty-string override, but describe_source treats the empty string as absent, falls through to a lower layer, and reports the wrong source for the value the caller is actually getting. This is the --explain command's output (per the docstring), so it silently misreports precedence on exactly the case the contract calls out as intentional. No test exercises an empty-string value.
findings.source: settings.py:5-8 (docstring: "A layer \"carries\" a key when the key is present, whatever the value -- an explicitly empty string is a deliberate override, not an absence.") vs settings.py:18 `if key in env:` (effective_value) and settings.py:28 `if env.get(key):` (describe_source); same drift repeats at settings.py:20/30 (project) and settings.py:22/32 (user)
findings.remedy: Make describe_source use the same presence check as effective_value (`if key in env: return "env"`, etc.) instead of truthiness, so both functions agree on what 'carries' means.

findings.claim: ORDER = ("env", "project", "user") is declared at module scope but never referenced anywhere in the file. Both effective_value and describe_source instead hard-code their own copy of the same three-layer sequence, which is how the two functions were free to drift onto different carries-checks (see the describe_source finding above) without either author needing to touch the other's code.
findings.source: settings.py:14 `ORDER = ("env", "project", "user")` (no other reference in file) vs the independently hard-coded sequences at settings.py:18-22 and settings.py:28-32
findings.remedy: Have both functions iterate ORDER against a {name: mapping} dict with one shared carries-check, so the precedence order and the definition of 'carries' are each expressed exactly once instead of twice.
